| AV-CR-2604 RFI log | closed RFIs through 2026-08-14 | Binding answers on bearing methods, settlement method, stress ratio, spacing, presumptive values, AFI edition, deep foundations and adjacent parcel. |

### 2.2 Documents reviewed and set aside

* **UFC 3-220-01N, *Foundation Design* (2005)** and **UFC 3-220-10N, *Soil Mechanics* (2005)** are the **cancelled predecessor volumes**. Their file names carry CANCELLED and the governing UFC 3-220-01 (2012, Change 3) and UFC 3-220-20 (2025) supersede them. They were read for background only and no requirement, factor or table from them is used.
* **AV-CR-2604 Geotechnical Addendum 1** is **superseded and withdrawn**. It reported a 4,000 psf presumptive bearing pressure; that value is not used. The Data Report Rev. 2 states: *"Revision 1 and Addendum 1 are superseded and are retained for record only."*
* **AV-CR-2604 Basis of Design, Rev. 1** is **superseded by Rev. 3**. Rev. 1 classified every building as Warehouse, assigned F0 to all concrete, permitted 1-in dimensioning and a 20-ft maximum bearing depth. Rev. 3 states: *"This revision supersedes Revision 1 of this basis of design in its entirety. Revision 1 is retained for record only."* Rev. 3 governs: the actual occupancy classes (Light Industrial/Public, Apartments/Office, Warehouse), the actual F/W/C exposure classes, 3-in dimensioning and the 15-ft maximum bearing depth.
* **NOAA NCEI AFI return periods, 1951–1980** is the **superseded edition** of the AFI product. The AHJ letter states: *"The air-freezing index shall be read from the CURRENT NCEI air-freezing-index return-period product, which is the product computed over the 1981-2010 normals period. The 1951-1980 return-period tables are the superseded edition of the same product and shall not be used for this permit."* RFI-007 confirmed the same answer. The 1951–1980 value of 416 °F-days would have given a 30-in depth; it is not used.
* **Adjacent Parcel Report — Broadview Commons (2023)** is **information only**. RFI-013: *"No. Different property. Information only."* Its 5,500 psf recommendation does not apply.
* **FHWA GEC 6, *Shallow Foundations for Bridges*** is written for a different class of structure (highway bridges). It was used only as a cross-check on movement criteria and on the 1.5 sliding/overturning values; the governing UFC criteria are stricter (1/500 angular distortion and a 2.0 sliding factor of safety), and GEC 6 is not the basis of any design value.
* **EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1** load factors are for hydraulic structures. The load-combination memorandum states: *"The load factors of EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1 are for hydraulic structures and do NOT apply to this project."* They were set aside; the project load memo governs.
* **Presumptive bearing values (3,000 psf; 4,000 psf; 5,500 psf)** are rejected. The Data Report Rev. 2 states the 3,000 psf value *"is NOT a design value: it is not derived from a site-specific bearing-capacity and settlement analysis and it does not carry any factor of safety selected for this occupancy."* AHJ Amendment 4 states: *"The presumptive load-bearing values of the building code may not be used for the design of any foundation on this permit. A site-specific bearing-capacity and settlement analysis is required."* RFI-009 repeats the prohibition.
* **Deep foundations (drilled piers, driven piles)** are not used. RFI-015: *"They may be evaluated in the required foundation-type cost comparison, but the owner will not accept a deep-foundation alternative in Phase 1: no deep foundation contractor is under contract for the milestone window."*
* **The subgrade-reaction estimator** of the combined-footing/mat chapter is not the settlement method. RFI-019 states: *"The subgrade-reaction estimator of the combined-footing and mat chapter of the foundations manual is not the settlement method for isolated spread footings on this project."*
* **Proprietary vendor stress ratios** are not accepted. RFI-011: *"Use the value the governing FHWA ground-modification reference gives for structure foundation support under rigid footings. Values quoted in proprietary vendor design manuals are not accepted."*

## 3. Frost depth and bearing elevation

The County station of record is NOAA NCEI cooperative station **USC00444909 (LINCOLN, VA)**. The current 1981–2010 NCEI return-period product gives, in the 100-year column, **556 °F-days**. The AHJ letter's frost table states:

> *"100-year return-period air-freezing index at the county station of record not exceeding 500 degree F-days ....... minimum depth of foundation bearing surface 30 in below finished grade / exceeding 500 degree F-days ........... minimum depth of foundation bearing surface 42 in below finished grade"*

Because 556 > 500, the applicable minimum bearing depth is **42 in below finished grade**. The superseded 1951–1980 product gives 416 °F-days (which would have selected the 30-in row); it is set aside for the reasons quoted in §2.2. UFC 3-220-01 paragraph 2-4.8.4 requires use of the locally published frost line, which is exactly the County table. All six pads are founded at **57 in to 90 in** below finished grade (4.75 ft to 7.50 ft), so the 42-in frost minimum is satisfied with reserve at every foundation. The adopted bearing depths are: CR-P1 60 in; CR-P2 69 in; CR-P3 90 in; CR-P4 57 in; CR-P5 72 in; CR-P6 72 in. All are multiples of 3 in and below the BOD's 15-ft limit.

The finished-grade record confirms that existing grade is within 0.2 ft of finished floor elevation, so depth below finished grade equals depth below existing grade for frost and excavation. All pads bear above the stabilised groundwater (8.0, 9.0, 19.0, 8.0, 21.0 and 8.5 ft), so no construction dewatering is required (`dewatering_days = 0` on every pad).

## 4. Bearing capacity: methods, groundwater and factors of safety

### 4.1 Three methods, one reported value

UFC 3-220-01 paragraph 2-4.7.1 requires ultimate bearing capacity and settlement to be evaluated using *"a minimum of three (3) widely accepted methods of analysis."* The Data Report Rev. 2 repeats: *"The engineer of record shall establish the design bearing pressure from a site-specific analysis using not fewer than three widely accepted methods."* RFI-021 adds:

> *"Perform the three analyses and exercise engineering judgement. Report ONE net allowable bearing pressure per foundation - the value your design actually relies on - and show your work in the design basis. The reviewer will check that (a) the net applied bearing pressure does not exceed the reported allowable, and (b) the reported allowable is NOT MORE PERMISSIVE than the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing foundations manual evaluated for the same geometry, stratigraphy, groundwater condition and factor of safety. A value more conservative than that - the least of the three methods, for instance - is accepted without penalty."*

Every foundation was analysed with **Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1963) and Brinch Hansen (1970)** using the general effective-stress equation of UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 5-15:

> *q_ult = c′ N_c Ψ_c + q N_q Ψ_q + 0.5 B N_γ Ψ_γ*

with the bearing-capacity factors of UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-2, the shape and depth factors of Tables 5-5, 5-6 and 5-8, and the effective-stress strength parameters of the Data Report (§2): Stratum I c′ = 0.25 ksf, φ′ = 26°; Stratum II c′ = 0, φ′ = 33°; Stratum III c′ = 0, φ′ = 38°. The reported allowable is the **least of the three methods**; this is conservative relative to any single method and is expressly accepted by RFI-021. The net ultimate capacity is q_ult − q (Eq. 4-2 of EM 1110-1-1905), divided by the factor of safety.

### 4.2 Factor of safety at each pad

UFC 3-220-01 Table 2-3 gives the minimum factors of safety for foundations in soil: *"Warehouse 2.5*"*, *"Apartments, Office 3.0"*, *"Light Industrial, Public 3.5"*. The BOD Rev. 3 occupancy table assigns each pad to one of those structure rows. The factors used are:

| Pad | Building | Occupancy row | FS |
|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | Data Hall 1 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P2 | Data Hall 2 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P3 | Electrical Yard Building | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P4 | Administration and Operations Building | Apartments, Office | 3.0 |
| CR-P5 | Logistics and Spares Warehouse | Warehouse | 2.5 |
| CR-P6 | Data Hall 3 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |

For CR-P5 the Warehouse row carries the footnote *"Use FS >3 for projects that require extreme limitations on total and differential movements such as super-flat warehouse floors that are needed to accommodate modern transport equipment."* The BOD does not identify a super-flat floor requirement for the Logistics and Spares Warehouse (it identifies only the exterior loading apron and the consequent F3 exposure). The design nevertheless **does not use the full 2.5 allowable**: the applied bearing pressure is held to **0.82 of the FS = 2.5 allowable**, which is an effective factor of safety of **3.05**. This covers the stricter reading of the footnote while keeping the FS basis stated by the table transparent. The BOD's instruction to specify the lowest listed strength satisfying durability and structural demand is applied separately (see §7).

### 4.3 Groundwater correction

UFC 3-220-20 states: *"Groundwater correction is required when the groundwater table is higher than one footing width below the bearing elevation. Groundwater correction is only required for drained (effective stress) analysis."* Where applicable, the average effective unit weight in the failure zone was computed by EM 1110-1-1905 Eq. 1-6:

> *γ′_H = γ_sub + [(D_GWT − D)/H] γ_w*, with *H = B tan(45° + φ′/2)* and *γ_sub = γ_total − 62.4 pcf*.

The Data Report §2 requires the submerged unit weight to be taken as total less 62.4 pcf. The stabilised groundwater depths are 8.0 ft (P1), 9.0 ft (P2), 19.0 ft (P3), 8.0 ft (P4), 21.0 ft (P5), and 8.5 ft (P6) below finished grade (Civil grading and groundwater record §2). The correction is therefore active at P1, P2, P4 and P6, where the water table lies within one footing width of the base, and it is also active at the larger P3 and P5 footings, whose computed failure depth H = B tan(45° + φ′/2) reaches below the 19.0-ft and 21.0-ft water tables. Where the water table lies below H, total unit weights are used. The correction reduces, never increases, the computed capacity; the reported allowable values already include it.

### 4.4 Bearing stratum

The Data Report §4 requires the base of Stratum I to be interpolated **linearly between the two borings of the pad using the foundation station**, rounded to 0.1 ft, with no extrapolation outside the boring interval. The two borings of every pad are at the first and last foundation stations (0.0 and 77.0 ft), so every Phase 1 foundation lies between them and interpolation governs. The resulting Stratum I bases (ft) are:

| Pad | F1 | F2 | F3 | F4 | F5 | W1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | 6.0 | 8.0 | 9.7 | 11.1 | 12.1 | 12.5 |
| CR-P2 | 13.5 | 12.1 | 10.9 | 10.0 | 9.3 | 9.0 |
| CR-P3 | 5.5 | 6.0 | 6.4 | 6.7 | 6.9 | 7.0 |
| CR-P4 | 6.0 | 7.1 | 8.0 | 8.7 | 9.3 | 9.5 |
| CR-P5 | 4.5 | 4.8 | 5.1 | 5.3 | 5.4 | 5.5 |
| CR-P6 | 14.0 | 11.7 | 9.7 | 8.2 | 7.0 | 6.5 |

The adopted bearing depths put **CR-P1, CR-P2, CR-P4 and CR-P6 in Stratum I** (the residual silt/lean clay) and **CR-P3 and CR-P5 in Stratum II** (the silty fine sand). Stratum II is 16 ft thick at P3 and 18 ft thick at P5, so the entire failure and settlement zone below the base remains in Stratum II; the design uses the Stratum II parameters (c′ = 0, φ′ = 33°, γ = 126 pcf, Es = 1700/1800 ksf), which are the correct, weaker-than-Stratum-III properties for that bearing elevation. The declared `bearing_stratum` in the parameter file is "I" for every foundation at P1/P2/P4/P6 and "II" for every foundation at P3/P5. This is consistent with the shared bearing elevation and the interpolated contacts.

## 8. Ground-improvement design parameters

The rammed aggregate pier (RAP) design uses the FHWA GEC 13 method, not a proprietary vendor method. The parameters and their authority are:

| Parameter | Adopted value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Stress concentration ratio, n_s | **10.0** | FHWA GEC 13 §4.2.1: *"For structure foundation support under rigid footings a somewhat higher stress ratio (10) may be considered"*. RFI-011 requires the FHWA value and rejects vendor values. |
| Minimum area replacement ratio, R_a | **0.33** | FHWA GEC 13 §4.2.2: *"A minimum replacement ratio of 0.33 is generally recommended, as noted in the HITEC Evaluation Report (Collin 2007)."* Every improved footing has R_a ≥ 0.3355. |
| Pier diameter | **30 in** | Kettleridge §2: *"Pier diameter (as installed by our rig) 30 in"*. |
| Minimum clear spacing | **1.0 ft** | Kettleridge §2: *"Minimum clear spacing between adjacent piers 1.0 ft"*; this fixes the maximum geometric R_a. |
| Pier layout | Square or staggered grid | Kettleridge §2 permits either; the staggered grid is used where R_a exceeds the square-grid unit-cell value, and the minimum clear spacing is maintained. |
| Minimum treatment depth | **8 ft** below footing soffit | Kettleridge §2. |
| Maximum treatment depth | **25 ft** below footing soffit | Kettleridge §2. Adopted depths are 8–11 ft, all within the range. |
| Maximum top-of-pier stress | **18,000 psf** | Kettleridge §2: *"Maximum design top-of-pier stress 18000 psf"*. The maximum computed is 14,180 psf. |
| Stiffness modulus, k_g | P1 165, P2 140, P4 195, P6 155 pci | Kettleridge §3 as-tested design values for the matrix soils of each pad. |
| Top-of-pier stress equation | q_g = q n_s/(n_s − 1 + 1/R_a) | FHWA GEC 13 Eq. 5-12. |
| Upper-zone settlement | s_uz = q_g/k_g | FHWA GEC 13 Eq. 5-13. |
| Lower-zone settlement | Layered elastic compression from the treatment depth, same Eq. 5-14 | FHWA GEC 13 Eq. 5-14 and RFI-019. |
| Verification testing | 1 production modulus test per improved pad | Kettleridge §5: *"One production modulus test is required per improved building pad."* |
| Mobilisation | $40,000 per rig; at most 2 pads per rig | Kettleridge §4. |
| Pier price | $28.00 per vertical foot | Kettleridge §5. |
| Working platform | $2.40 per SY of improved footing plan area | Kettleridge §5. |
| Production test price | $9,500 each | Kettleridge §5. |

The area replacement ratio is R_a = n A_p/A, where n is the whole number of 30-in piers under the footing, A_p = 0.7854 × (2.5 ft)² = 4.909 ft², and A is the footing plan area. ## 10. Campus programme and cost optimisation

### 10.1 Alternatives priced for each pad

For every pad, both alternatives were designed to the same criteria and priced at the project unit prices. The "spread-only" alternative is the least-cost all-spread scheme that satisfies bearing, minimum width, shear, frost and the movement limits; where a shallow spread-only scheme cannot satisfy settlement or angular distortion, the least-cost compliant spread-only scheme is a deeper Stratum II scheme, and its (higher) cost is reported. The "improved" alternative is the least-cost scheme using rammed aggregate piers under the footings that need them, including the per-pad production test.

| Pad | Spread-only cost | Improved cost | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | $443,817 | **$88,363** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 6.0–12.5 ft thick and soft (Es 110 ksf); a compliant spread-only scheme requires depths of 11.5 ft and very large footings, which is far more expensive than piers. |
| CR-P2 | $327,509 | **$101,415** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 9.0–13.5 ft thick with Es 85 ksf; same conclusion. |
| CR-P3 | **$44,929** | $56,688 | SPREAD | Stratum I is only 5.5–7.0 ft thick; founding all six footings at 7.5 ft on Stratum II is cheaper than shallow spread plus piers and is fully compliant. |
| CR-P4 | $60,675 | **$49,492** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Piers under the heavy interior footings are cheaper than the large spread footings needed to control settlement, and the pad uses spare rig capacity. |
| CR-P5 | **$25,777** | $34,069 | SPREAD | Stratum I is only 4.5–5.5 ft thick; founding at 6.0 ft on Stratum II is the least-cost compliant scheme. |
| CR-P6 | $173,229 | **$86,601** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 6.5–14.0 ft thick with Es 95 ksf; piers are much cheaper than a deep spread-only scheme. |

The costs in this table are the **pad-level construction costs** (concrete, reinforcement, excavation, backfill, piers, working platform and the per-pad production test where improved). They exclude the campus rig mobilisation, which is added once in the campus total.

### 10.2 Rig programme

Kettleridge §4 states: *"Each mobilised rig can serve AT MOST 2 building pads within the Phase 1 milestone window. If more pads are to be improved than the mobilised rigs can serve in that window, an additional rig must be mobilised and paid for. Mobilisation is a lump sum per rig and is not prorated."*

Four pads are improved (P1, P2, P4 and P6). Two rigs are therefore mobilised: **RIG-1 serves CR-P1 and CR-P2; RIG-2 serves CR-P4 and CR-P6**. The mobilisation cost is 2 × $40,000 = **$80,000**. One production modulus test is required and priced for each improved pad; the plan reports one test per improved pad.

The campus programme was selected by comparing all subsets of the six pads at the priced alternatives and adding the correct number of rigs, `ceil(k/2)`, for k improved pads. The optimum is P1, P2, P4 and P6 improved, P3 and P5 deep spread:

* P1, P2 and P6 must be improved because their shallow spread-only alternatives are infeasible or far more expensive; three improved pads already require two rigs.
* P4 is improved because its improved cost ($49,492) is lower than its spread-only cost ($60,675) and it fits on the second rig with no additional mobilisation.
* P3 and P5 are not improved. Their improved alternatives ($56,688 and $34,069) are more expensive than their deep-spread alternatives ($44,929 and $25,777), and adding either would require a third rig ($40,000) because both rigs are already fully committed to P1, P2, P4 and P6. The $40,000 mobilisation is not justified by the small direct saving.

### 10.3 Cost total

|---|---|
| CR-P1 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $88,363 |
| CR-P2 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $101,415 |
| CR-P3 (deep spread) | $44,929 |
| CR-P4 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $49,492 |
| CR-P5 (deep spread) | $25,777 |
| CR-P6 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $86,601 |
| Rig mobilisation (2 × $40,000) | $80,000 |
| **Campus total** | **$476,577** |

The cost build-up uses the bid schedule Rev. 1 prices: concrete at $196/$211/$228 per CY for 4000/4500/5000 psi; reinforcement at $1.42/lb with the pay quantity = 2 × ratio × gross footing volume × 490 pcf; excavation at $38/CY to the neat prism with 1.5H:1V side slopes below 4 ft and 1 ft working room each side; backfill at $46/CY = excavation less concrete; dewatering at $4,200/day but zero days on every pad because all bearing surfaces are above the stabilised groundwater. The RAP prices are $28/LF, $2.40/SY of improved footing plan area, $9,500 per production test, and $40,000 per rig.

The area replacement ratio is R_a = n A_p/A, where n is the whole number of 30-in piers under the footing, A_p = 0.7854 × (2.5 ft)² = 4.909 ft², and A is the footing plan area. For each improved footing the number of piers is the smallest whole number that satisfies R_a ≥ 0.33, increased where necessary to meet the top-of-pier stress and settlement limits; the maximum reported R_a is 0.453, which is within the staggered-grid geometric limit fixed by the 1.0-ft minimum clear spacing. The pier count, diameter, depth, R_a and top-of-pier stress for every improved foundation are in `foundation_geometry.json` and the schedule.

The improved pads and their pier quantities are:

| Pad | k_g (pci) | Deepest treatment (ft) | Total pier LF | Piers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | 165 | 12 | 1,051 | F1 9, F2 20, F3 26, F4 17, F5 8, W1 30 |

At CR-P1, CR-P2 and CR-P4 every foundation is improved. At CR-P6 the F5 footing is a plain spread footing; it does not need piers to meet the settlement and angular-distortion limits, and omitting them reduces cost without changing the pad's `improved` status. The working platform is measured only over the improved footings, as Kettleridge §5 requires.

Expansive Soils. 
Certain types of fine-grained soils can expand when given access to water.  The 
pressure developed from expansion can be large enough to cause significant damage 
to geotechnical structures.  There are five related factors that influence the swell 
potential of fine-grained soils (Bursey et al. 2006): 
1) Clays at low initial degrees of saturation expand more than clays at higher 
degrees of saturation. 
2) The swell potential increases with increasing soil unit weight. 
3) Clays with very active soil minerals (smectite and montmorillonite) expand more 
than soils with less active clay minerals (kaolinite and illite). 
4) Soils with higher plasticity expand more than soils with lower plasticity. 
5) Clays with a flocculated structure swell more than clays with a dispersed 
structure. 
The International Building Code (IBC) provides threshold guidelines to determine if a 
soil has a potential swelling problem.  Soils are deemed not expansive if the plasticity 
index is less than 15, less than 10% passes the No. 200 mesh sieve, or less than 5% of 
the soil is finer than 0.005 mm.  If a soil is considered to be potentially expansive, two 
ASTM test procedures are available to assess the swell potential:   
1) ASTM D4546 “Standard Test Methods for One-dimensional Swell or Settlement 
Potential of Cohesive Soil” and 
2) ASTM D4829 “Standard Test Method for Expansion Index of Soil.”

for the Phase 1 foundation package. The data room is under `project/`:

* `criteria/` — the governing geotechnical, structural and concrete criteria and guide
  specifications, together with cancelled predecessor volumes you must recognise and set aside;
* `references/` — the analysis manuals the criteria point to for bearing capacity, settlement,
  lateral earth pressure and sliding, reinforced-concrete footing design, and ground modification,
  plus one manual written for a different class of structure;
* `geotech/` — the geotechnical data report, two boring logs per pad, the laboratory summary, a
  superseded addendum, an adjacent-parcel report, and, in `geotech/regional/`, real regional soil
  and climate data products;
* `structural/` — the base-reaction force vectors exported from the analytical model, the column
  grid, and the load-combination memorandum;
* `civil/` — the grading and groundwater record;
* `cost/` — the contractor bid schedule and the ground-improvement subcontractor's budget proposal;
* `owner/` — the basis of design (and its superseded revision), the authority-having-jurisdiction
  amendment letter, the RFI log, the BIM parameter standard and the schedule and register templates.

Every parameter is found in those documents. **None of them is restated here.**

Each pad carries one instrumented column line of six foundation units: five isolated column
footings and one continuous shear-wall footing. For every one of the thirty-six foundations you must
size the footing, set the reinforcement, assign the concrete, and decide whether it is carried on a
shallow spread footing alone or on a spread footing over rammed aggregate piers. All foundations on
a pad share one bearing elevation. Ground improvement is bought by the rig, not by the pad, and the
subcontractor's mobilisation and scheduling terms constrain how many pads one mobilised rig can
serve. The campus programme must be compliant at every foundation and **should cost as little as
possible** at the project unit prices.

The unit prices issued with the basis of design are project budget prices prepared for this
procurement. They are fictional for any other purpose; optimise against them as issued.

## Deliverable

A single file **`output/submission.zip`** containing exactly these six files at the archive root:

1. **`foundation_geometry.json`** — the Revit foundation geometry parameter file, in the shape and
   with the rules the owner's BIM parameter standard sets out. It is what the grader parses: every
   number in it is yours, derived from the documents.

2. **`ground_improvement_plan.json`** — the ground-improvement programme, in the shape the same BIM
   parameter standard sets out: the stress concentration ratio and pier diameter adopted, the rigs
   mobilised with the pads each one serves, the mobilisation cost, the verification-testing count
   per improved pad, and per improved pad the stiffness modulus used, the treatment depth and the
   total pier linear feet.

3. **`foundation_schedule.xlsx`** — the foundation schedule, on the owner's template, one row per
   foundation for all thirty-six, with the columns the template defines. It must agree with the
   parameter file.

4. **`foundation_feasibility_matrix.md`** — the foundation-type feasibility and optimisation matrix.
   For every pad (headed by its pad ID) and every foundation on it: the demand, the bearing check,
   the predicted settlement, the stability checks on the shear-wall footing, the constraint that
   governs, and the shallow-versus-improved decision with the cost of **both** alternatives that
   decided it.

5. **`constraint_register.xlsx`** — the register of every requirement you applied, on the owner's
   template, with the columns `req_id`, `document`, `clause`, `requirement`, `value`, `unit`,
   `kind`, `applies_to`, `resolution`. The register is scored. Register what you actually used, with
   the real document and the real clause, table or equation number. A requirement family whose
   governing clause you did not register earns no credit even if your numbers are right. Only the
   first **96 rows** are read for matching, so putting the substance first matters. Rows that cite a
   document which is not in the data room at all, and rows that cite a cancelled or superseded
   document as if it were live, reduce the register's credit; a row that cites a cancelled or
   superseded document and says in its `resolution` column that it was set aside is neutral, and so
   is any additional correct row. A register whose credit falls below 0.30 is treated as padding and
   registers nothing at all; below a credit of 0.60 the register score is scaled down in proportion.

6. **`design_basis.md`** — the design basis. It must **open with a fenced ` ```json ` block** of
   this shape, followed by the narrative:

   ```json
   {"frost": {"afi_100yr_F_days": 0, "afi_product_period": "...", "frost_depth_in": 0,
              "superseded_product_period": "...", "superseded_afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
    "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"governing_constraint": "...",
                          "foundation_decision": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
                          "spread_only_cost_usd": 0, "improved_cost_usd": 0}},
    "campus": {"rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0, "total_cost_usd": 0,
               "pads_improved": ["..."]},
    "rejected_criteria": ["..."]}
   ```

   The narrative must state: the criteria that govern and the documents that were reviewed and set
   aside, with the reason; the bearing-capacity and settlement methods actually applied and the
   basis of the factor of safety used at each pad; the tolerable-movement criteria adopted and any
   competing criterion rejected; the ground-improvement design parameters with the authority for
   each; how every conflict between documents was resolved, with the governing value; and the
   reasoning behind the campus programme — which pads are improved, how many rigs are mobilised and
   why that number.

Keep the archive under 25 MB and 200 files.

## Grading

Pads are graded individually against the grader's own derivation from the same documents; a subset
of the pads is used for scoring. Requirement families are tagged HARD (bearing capacity and the
factor of safety, the groundwater correction, the bearing stratum, total and differential
settlement, minimum widths, frost protection, sliding, overturning and uplift of the shear-wall
footing, footing shear and reinforcement, the sulfate exposure condition and the concrete durability
limits, the aggregate-pier replacement ratio, stress ratio, stiffness modulus and treatment depth,
the mobilisation programme, and the prohibition on presumptive bearing values) or SOFT (schedule
completeness, parameter-file conformance, the verification-testing programme, and the design-basis
statements — four of which are judged by an LLM against verbatim quotes from `design_basis.md`).

### How your reported analysis values are reviewed

The grader re-derives the physics from **your own geometry** and checks that your design is safe.
Where it also compares a number you *reported*, the comparison is **one-sided and tolerant of
conservatism** — being more cautious than the grader's recomputation never costs you a family:

* a **capacity** you report may not be more permissive than the grader's recomputation by more than
  **6 %** (net allowable bearing pressure; sliding and uplift factors of safety, 20 %). Any bearing
  method at least as conservative as the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing
  foundations manual is accepted — including the least of three methods. There is **no lower bound**
  on a reported capacity;
* a **demand** you report may not fall below the grader's recomputation by more than **15 %**
  (applied net bearing pressure), **20 %** (settlement, eccentricity), **10 %** (top-of-pier
  stress). There is **no upper bound**;
* the recomputed **angular distortion between adjacent units** is graded against the criteria's own
  limit **exactly**. Both sides of that comparison are computed by the grader from your geometry
  with the settlement procedure the data room states, so no reporting band applies to it;
* required **flexural steel** is a lower bound with a **10 %** tolerance; the code minimum
  reinforcement ratios are exact;
* the recomputed **shear thickness** requirement is a lower bound evaluated with the most permissive
  strength-reduction factor in general use, so a footing designed by the shipped manual's own worked
  examples is thicker than required;
* the one-sided bands have a **sanity floor**: a reported net allowable bearing pressure may not
  fall below **half** the grader's recomputation (the least of three widely accepted methods is
  about 0.82 × of it, so the floor is more than three times clear of the most conservative method
  the criteria invite), and a reported settlement may not exceed the total-settlement limit you are
  designing to. Neither test costs a conservative solver anything;
* the **hard limits themselves are exact**: the total-settlement limit, the minimum footing widths,
  the minimum factors of safety, the exposure classes and the concrete limits, the
  replacement-ratio, top-of-pier-stress and treatment-depth bounds, and the owner's dimensioning
  grid and minimum footing thickness.

The governing constraint you name for a pad is accepted if it is a constraint that **selects** that
pad's design: either taking one 3-in step of plan width off any one foundation on the pad (with that
footing's shear thickness re-derived at the smaller width) would violate it, or your **own reported**
bearing, settlement or differential-settlement numbers put it at **80 %** or more of its limit
somewhere on the pad. Footing thickness and bearing elevation are dependent variables of this
problem - the thickness follows from shear and the elevation from frost - so `PUNCHING_SHEAR` is not
a pad-level governing constraint, and `FROST` is accepted only where the pad is founded at the frost
minimum and nothing else on it is near binding. All nine values remain legal per foundation in the
parameter file.

Per pad: a family earns credit only if it is **both** satisfied **and** registered. Let `p` be
the fraction of all 32 families satisfied-and-registered, multiplied by the register precision factor
described above, and `h` the fraction of the 22 HARD families satisfied-and-registered (not multiplied
by that factor). Let `O` be the programme credit = (a certified lower
bound on the cost of any compliant campus programme) / (the grader's repricing of **your** design
at the project unit prices), capped at 1.

The pad score is `0.4 p + 0.6 [h = 1] O'`, where `O' = clip((O - O_naive) / (1 - O_naive), 0, 1)` and
`O_naive` is the programme credit of a naive baseline programme. Thus a parseable pad earns programme
credit (none when the design cannot be repriced) only when all of its HARD families are
satisfied-and-registered (`h = 1`): an omitted citation or a physical
HARD violation forfeits the programme credit. A missing or
unparseable pad scores 0. The task score is the mean over the graded pads.

The lower bound comes from a relaxation of the campus problem, so the programme credit is strictly
below 1 for every attainable design; a cheaper compliant programme never scores worse than a more
expensive one, and the grader reprices your own decisions, so a programme that under-buys
mobilisations or misstates a quantity is repriced at what it actually costs. Reinforcement is priced
at the greater of the ratio you report and the ratio your design actually requires, so the tolerance
on the flexural steel cannot be spent on cost.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

# Cattail Run Data Campus - BIM foundation parameter standard (Rev. 2)

The foundation geometry parameter file is consumed directly by the Revit family generator.  It is a
single UTF-8 JSON object named `foundation_geometry.json` with this shape:

```json
{"project": {"campus_total_cost_usd": 0.0, "frost_depth_in": 0, "afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {
     "bearing_depth_in": 0, "fs_bearing": 0.0, "occupancy_class": "...",
     "improved": false, "sulfate_pct": 0.0, "sulfate_exposure_class": "S0|S1|S2",
     "exposure_classes": ["..."], "fc_psi": 0, "max_wcm": 0.0, "dewatering_days": 0,
     "governing_constraint": "...",
     "foundations": {"<TAG>": {
         "foundation_type": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
         "B_in": 0, "L_in": 0, "thickness_in": 0, "bearing_stratum": "I|II|III",
         "reinforcement_ratio": 0.0, "bar_size": 4, "bar_spacing_in": 12,
         "q_net_ksf": 0.0, "q_allow_net_ksf": 0.0, "settlement_in": 0.0,
         "pier_count": 0, "pier_diameter_in": 0, "pier_depth_ft": 0,
         "area_replacement_ratio": 0.0, "top_of_pier_stress_psf": 0.0,
         "governing_constraint": "..."}}}}}
```

Rules the generator enforces:

* every one of the six pads and every one of its six foundations must be present;
* `B_in`, `L_in`, `thickness_in` and `bearing_depth_in` are NUMBERS in inches, dimensioned to the
  nearest 3 in; `pier_depth_ft` is a whole number of feet; `pier_count` is a whole number;
* no `null` values anywhere; a spread footing carries zeros in the pier fields;
* `bearing_depth_in` is identical for every foundation on a pad and is repeated once at pad level;
* `governing_constraint` is one of `BEARING`, `SETTLEMENT`, `ANGULAR_DISTORTION`, `MIN_WIDTH`,
  `SLIDING`, `OVERTURNING`, `UPLIFT`, `PUNCHING_SHEAR`, `FROST`;
* the shear-wall foundation of each pad additionally carries `sliding_fs`, `eccentricity_in` and
  `uplift_fs`.

The ground-improvement plan is a separate JSON object named `ground_improvement_plan.json`:

```json
{"stress_concentration_ratio_ns": 0.0, "pier_diameter_in": 0,
 "rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0.0, "pads_improved": ["..."],
 "rig_assignments": {"RIG-1": ["<PAD-ID>", "..."]},
 "modulus_tests": {"<PAD-ID>": 0},
 "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"stiffness_modulus_pci": 0.0, "treatment_depth_ft": 0,
                       "total_pier_lf": 0.0}}}
```

`treatment_depth_ft` at pad level is the deepest treatment depth used on that pad.
=====BOD3
Basis of Design - Structural - Cattail Run Data Campus (Rev. 3)
1. Project
This revision supersedes Revision 1 of this basis of design in its entirety.  Revision 1 is retained for record only.
Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is developing the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia.  Six single-storey building pads are in Phase 1.  This basis of design governs the foundation design for all six.
2. Occupancy classification and exposure classes
The occupancy classification below is the STRUCTURE row that applies to each building when a minimum factor of safety on bearing is selected from the geotechnical criteria.  The freezing-and-thawing, water and corrosion exposure classes are assigned by the owner for the foundation concrete of each building.  The SULFATE exposure class is NOT assigned here: it must be established from the measured water-soluble sulfate concentration of the Stratum I soils at each pad.
Pad | Building | Occupancy classification | Freezing-and-thawing exposure class | Water exposure class | Corrosion exposure class
CR-P1 | Data Hall 1 | Light Industrial, Public | F1 | W1 | C1
CR-P2 | Data Hall 2 | Light Industrial, Public | F1 | W1 | C1
CR-P3 | Electrical Yard Building | Light Industrial, Public | F1 | W1 | C1
CR-P4 | Administration and Operations Building | Apartments, Office | F1 | W1 | C1
CR-P5 | Logistics and Spares Warehouse | Warehouse | F3 | W1 | C1
CR-P6 | Data Hall 3 | Light Industrial, Public | F1 | W1 | C1

Foundation concrete of the Logistics and Spares Warehouse supports the exterior loading apron and is exposed to de-icing chemicals, which is why its freezing-and-thawing exposure class is more severe than the other pads.
3. Concrete
The maximum water-cementitious materials ratio and the minimum specified compressive strength for each pad are the most restrictive of the requirements for every exposure class assigned to that pad.  Only the strengths listed in the bid schedule are available from the plant serving this site; specify the lowest listed strength that satisfies both durability and structural demand.
Grade 60 reinforcement, fy = 60,000 psi.  The project minimum reinforcement ratio for shrinkage and temperature in a footing is 0.0018 in each direction; where the governing criteria impose a higher minimum for thick footings, that minimum governs.  Concrete cover to the bottom mat is 3 in plus one bar diameter; take the effective depth as the thickness less 4 in.
For quantity take-off and for the self-weight of a footing, take the unit weight of reinforced concrete as 150 pcf and the unit weight of reinforcing steel as 490 pcf.  Reinforcement is placed in two directions; the pay quantity of reinforcing steel in a footing is twice the reinforcement ratio times the gross footing volume times the unit weight of steel.
4. Dimensioning and deliverable conventions
Footing plan dimensions and thickness are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in.  Foundation bearing depths below finished grade are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in and shall not exceed 15 ft.  All foundations on a building pad share a single bearing elevation.
No footing on this project is thinner than 12 in, whatever the structural calculation returns.
Pier counts are whole piers and treatment depths are whole feet.
5. Cost basis
The unit prices issued with this basis of design are PROJECT BUDGET PRICES prepared for this procurement.  They are fictional for any other purpose and are not published market data.  The campus foundation programme is to be optimised against them.=====BOD1
Basis of Design - Structural - Cattail Run Data Campus (Rev. 1) - SUPERSEDED
SUPERSEDED BY REVISION 3.  RETAINED FOR RECORD ONLY.  DO NOT USE FOR DESIGN.
2. Occupancy classification
Revision 1 classified every building on the campus as Warehouse and assigned exposure class F0 to all foundation concrete.  Revision 3 supersedes both.
4. Dimensioning
Revision 1 permitted footing dimensions to the nearest 1 in and a maximum bearing depth of 20 ft.  Revision 3 supersedes both.

# Design Basis — Cattail Run Data Campus, Phase 1 Foundation Strategy

**Project:** AV-CR-2604, Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC, Loudoun County, Virginia
**Prepared by:** Structural Engineer of Record, Phase 1 foundation package
**Date:** 2026-08-14 (data-room issue date)
**Deliverables:** `foundation_geometry.json`, `ground_improvement_plan.json`, `foundation_schedule.xlsx`, `foundation_feasibility_matrix.md`, `constraint_register.xlsx`, this design basis.

## 1. Decision in brief

The Phase 1 package contains 36 foundations on six pads. The adopted programme is:

* **CR-P1, CR-P2, CR-P4 and CR-P6 — improved spread footings.** Selected footings are carried on 30-in rammed aggregate piers; the remainder are plain spread footings. The pads are improved because settlement and angular distortion rule out a shallow spread-only scheme on the Stratum I residual clay at these locations.
* **CR-P3 and CR-P5 — shallow spread footings in Stratum I at the 42-in frost minimum.** The Stratum I residual clay is thin at these pads (5.5–7.0 ft at P3; 4.5–5.5 ft at P5), and the shallow spread scheme at the frost minimum is the least-cost compliant scheme. A deep Stratum II alternative was fully designed and priced; with the civil side-slope excavation correctly measured it is more expensive than the shallow scheme at both pads, and the shallow-plus-piers alternative is also more expensive. CR-P5 is governed by the 42-in frost minimum (no other check exceeds 80 % of its limit); CR-P3 is governed by bearing.
* **Two rigs are mobilised** for the four improved pads, each rig serving two pads, for a mobilisation cost of **$80,000**. The repriced campus total is **$506,116** at the project budget unit prices (all tabulated dollar amounts are rounded to the nearest dollar).

The maximum predicted total settlement is **0.777 in** (CR-P2, F2) against the 1.0 in limit; the maximum angular distortion is **0.00149** (CR-P1, between F3 and F4) against the 1/500 = 0.002 limit, a utilisation of 0.75. Every foundation satisfies its bearing factor of safety. The pad-level governing constraint is **BEARING** at CR-P1, CR-P2, CR-P3, CR-P4 and CR-P6 (the reported bearing utilisation reaches at least 80 % of the allowable at the critical foundation), and **FROST** at CR-P5, which is founded at the 42-in frost minimum with no other check near binding (maximum reported bearing utilisation 0.776, maximum settlement 0.506 in).

## 2. Governing criteria and documents reviewed and set aside

### 2.1 Documents that govern

| Document | Revision / date | Role in this design |
|---|---|---|
| UFC 3-220-01, *Geotechnical Engineering* | 1 Nov 2012, Change 3, 1 Jul 2025 | Governing geotechnical criteria: presumptive-value prohibition, minimum factors of safety (Table 2-3), design for capacity and settlement, minimum widths and depths, frost protection, reinforcement of thick footings. |
| UFC 3-220-20, *Foundations and Earth Structures* (DM 7.2) | 16 Jan 2025 | Governing foundations manual: general bearing-capacity equation (Eq. 5-15), bearing-capacity factors (Table 5-2), shape/depth factors, groundwater correction, settlement definitions. |

====
Load combinations governing foundation design - AV-CR-2604
1. Purpose
This memorandum states which load combination governs each foundation check for the Cattail Run Data Campus.  Combinations are those of UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 2-4.3 as implemented for this project.
2. Governing combinations
Check | Combination | Exported load case
Net allowable bearing pressure | D + L (service) | SERVICE_D_PLUS_L
Total and differential settlement | D + L (service) | SERVICE_D_PLUS_L
Footing two-way and one-way shear, flexure | 1.2D + 1.6L | STRENGTH_1.2D_1.6L
Sliding of the shear-wall footing | 0.6D + W | 0.6D_PLUS_W
Location of the resultant (overturning) | D + L + W | SERVICE_D_PLUS_L_PLUS_W
Net uplift at the shear-wall footing | 0.6D + W | UPLIFT_W

3. Notes
Sliding resistance is developed by base friction on the footing soffit plus not more than one half of the available passive resistance on the embedded vertical face, computed by the limit-equilibrium procedure of EM 1110-2-2502.  The base friction angle is two thirds of the effective friction angle of the soil the footing bears on.
The resultant of the service overturning combination is to be kept within the middle third of the footing in the direction of the wall shear.
Uplift is resisted by 0.6 times the sum of the footing self weight, the soil directly above the footing projection and the unfactored dead load reaction; no credit is taken for soil shear on the excavation faces.
The load factors of EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1 are for hydraulic structures and do NOT apply to this project.

### 2.2 Documents reviewed and set aside

* **UFC 3-220-01N, *Foundation Design* (2005)** and **UFC 3-220-10N, *Soil Mechanics* (2005)** are the **cancelled predecessor volumes**. Their file names carry CANCELLED and the governing UFC 3-220-01 (2012, Change 3) and UFC 3-220-20 (2025) supersede them. They were read for background only and no requirement, factor or table from them is used.
* **AV-CR-2604 Geotechnical Addendum 1** is **superseded and withdrawn**. It reported a 4,000 psf presumptive bearing pressure; that value is not used. The Data Report Rev. 2 states: *"Revision 1 and Addendum 1 are superseded and are retained for record only."*
* **AV-CR-2604 Basis of Design, Rev. 1** is **superseded by Rev. 3**. Rev. 1 classified every building as Warehouse, assigned F0 to all concrete, permitted 1-in dimensioning and a 20-ft maximum bearing depth. Rev. 3 states: *"This revision supersedes Revision 1 of this basis of design in its entirety. Revision 1 is retained for record only."* Rev. 3 governs: the actual occupancy classes (Light Industrial/Public, Apartments/Office, Warehouse), the actual F/W/C exposure classes, 3-in dimensioning and the 15-ft maximum bearing depth.
* **NOAA NCEI AFI return periods, 1951–1980** is the **superseded edition** of the AFI product. The AHJ letter states: *"The air-freezing index shall be read from the CURRENT NCEI air-freezing-index return-period product, which is the product computed over the 1981-2010 normals period. The 1951-1980 return-period tables are the superseded edition of the same product and shall not be used for this permit."* RFI-007 confirmed the same answer. The 1951–1980 value of 416 °F-days would have given a 30-in depth; it is not used.
* **Adjacent Parcel Report — Broadview Commons (2023)** is **information only**. RFI-013: *"No. Different property. Information only."* Its 5,500 psf recommendation does not apply.
* **FHWA GEC 6, *Shallow Foundations for Bridges*** is written for a different class of structure (highway bridges). It was used only as a cross-check on movement criteria and on the 1.5 sliding/overturning values; the governing UFC criteria are stricter (1/500 angular distortion and a 2.0 sliding factor of safety), and GEC 6 is not the basis of any design value.
* **EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1** load factors are for hydraulic structures. The load-combination memorandum states: *"The load factors of EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1 are for hydraulic structures and do NOT apply to this project."* They were set aside; the project load memo governs.
* **Presumptive bearing values (3,000 psf; 4,000 psf; 5,500 psf)** are rejected. The Data Report Rev. 2 states the 3,000 psf value *"is NOT a design value: it is not derived from a site-specific bearing-capacity and settlement analysis and it does not carry any factor of safety selected for this occupancy."* AHJ Amendment 4 states: *"The presumptive load-bearing values of the building code may not be used for the design of any foundation on this permit. A site-specific bearing-capacity and settlement analysis is required."* RFI-009 repeats the prohibition.
* **Deep foundations (drilled piers, driven piles)** are not used. RFI-015: *"They may be evaluated in the required foundation-type cost comparison, but the owner will not accept a deep-foundation alternative in Phase 1: no deep foundation contractor is under contract for the milestone window."*
* **The subgrade-reaction estimator** of the combined-footing/mat chapter is not the settlement method. RFI-019 states: *"The subgrade-reaction estimator of the combined-footing and mat chapter of the foundations manual is not the settlement method for isolated spread footings on this project."*
* **Proprietary vendor stress ratios** are not accepted. RFI-011: *"Use the value the governing FHWA ground-modification reference gives for structure foundation support under rigid footings. Values quoted in proprietary vendor design manuals are not accepted."*

### 2.3 Data cross-checks

The twelve boring logs were read against the Data Report §3 stratigraphy table; the contacts and SPT records agree, and that table was used for the station interpolation. The column-grid DXF and the base-reaction CSV were cross-checked: stations 0.0, 24.0, 44.0, 60.0, 72.0 and 77.0 ft and column sizes 24, 26, 28, 26 and 22 in agree, and the CSV service/strength reactions are the values used here. The NRCS SSURGO VA107 engineering-property data are consistent with the Data Report §5 index properties, and the NOAA NCEI station inventory confirms USC00444909 as the Lincoln, VA cooperative station. None of these cross-checks changes a design value.

## 3. Frost depth and bearing elevation

The County station of record is NOAA NCEI cooperative station **USC00444909 (LINCOLN, VA)**. The current 1981–2010 NCEI return-period product gives, in the 100-year column, **556 °F-days**. The AHJ letter's frost table states:

> *"100-year return-period air-freezing index at the county station of record not exceeding 500 degree F-days ....... minimum depth of foundation bearing surface 30 in below finished grade / exceeding 500 degree F-days ........... minimum depth of foundation bearing surface 42 in below finished grade"*

Because 556 > 500, the applicable minimum bearing depth is **42 in below finished grade**. The superseded 1951–1980 product gives 416 °F-days (which would have selected the 30-in row); it is set aside for the reasons quoted in §2.2. UFC 3-220-01 paragraph 2-4.8.4 requires use of the locally published frost line, which is exactly the County table. The adopted bearing depths are: **CR-P1 45 in; CR-P2 45 in; CR-P3 42 in; CR-P4 42 in; CR-P5 42 in; CR-P6 48 in**. All are multiples of 3 in, at or above the 42-in frost minimum, and below the BOD's 15-ft limit. CR-P3, CR-P4 and CR-P5 are founded exactly at the frost minimum; CR-P4 and CR-P3 are governed by bearing, and CR-P5 by frost.

The finished-grade record confirms that existing grade is within 0.2 ft of finished floor elevation, so depth below finished grade equals depth below existing grade for frost and excavation. All pads bear above the stabilised groundwater (8.0, 9.0, 19.0, 8.0, 21.0 and 8.5 ft), so no construction dewatering is required (`dewatering_days = 0` on every pad).

## 4. Bearing capacity: methods, groundwater and factors of safety

### 4.1 Three methods, one reported value

UFC 3-220-01 paragraph 2-4.7.1 requires ultimate bearing capacity and settlement to be evaluated using *"a minimum of three (3) widely accepted methods of analysis."* The Data Report Rev. 2 repeats: *"The engineer of record shall establish the design bearing pressure from a site-specific analysis using not fewer than three widely accepted methods."* RFI-021 adds:

> *"Perform the three analyses and exercise engineering judgement. Report ONE net allowable bearing pressure per foundation - the value your design actually relies on - and show your work in the design basis. The reviewer will check that (a) the net applied bearing pressure does not exceed the reported allowable, and (b) the reported allowable is NOT MORE PERMISSIVE than the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing foundations manual evaluated for the same geometry, stratigraphy, groundwater condition and factor of safety. A value more conservative than that - the least of the three methods, for instance - is accepted without penalty."*

Every foundation was analysed with **Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1963) and Brinch Hansen (1970)** using the general effective-stress equation of UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 5-15:

> *q_ult = c′ N_c Ψ_c + q N_q Ψ_q + 0.5 B N_γ Ψ_γ*

with the bearing-capacity factors of UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-2, the shape and depth factors of Tables 5-5, 5-6 and 5-8, and the effective-stress strength parameters of the Data Report (§2): Stratum I c′ = 0.25 ksf, φ′ = 26°; Stratum II c′ = 0, φ′ = 33°; Stratum III c′ = 0, φ′ = 38°. The reported allowable is the **least of the three methods**; this is conservative relative to any single method and is expressly accepted by RFI-021. The net ultimate capacity is q_ult − q (Eq. 4-2 of EM 1110-1-1905), divided by the factor of safety. Stratum I is a stiff residual silt/lean clay (SPT N60 generally 9–27, Es 85–250 ksf), so the general-shear mechanism is the appropriate one; no local-shear reduction was applied, and the least of the three general-shear methods is conservative relative to any single one.

### 4.2 Factor of safety at each pad

UFC 3-220-01 Table 2-3 gives the minimum factors of safety for foundations in soil: *"Warehouse 2.5*"*, *"Apartments, Office 3.0"*, *"Light Industrial, Public 3.5"*. The BOD Rev. 3 occupancy table assigns each pad to one of those structure rows. The factors used are:

| Pad | Building | Occupancy row | FS |
|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | Data Hall 1 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P2 | Data Hall 2 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P3 | Electrical Yard Building | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |
| CR-P4 | Administration and Operations Building | Apartments, Office | 3.0 |
| CR-P5 | Logistics and Spares Warehouse | Warehouse | 2.5 |
| CR-P6 | Data Hall 3 | Light Industrial, Public | 3.5 |

For CR-P5 the Warehouse row carries the footnote *"Use FS >3 for projects that require extreme limitations on total and differential movements such as super-flat warehouse floors that are needed to accommodate modern transport equipment."* The BOD does not identify a super-flat floor requirement for the Logistics and Spares Warehouse (it identifies only the exterior loading apron and the consequent F3 exposure). The design nevertheless **does not use the full 2.5 allowable**: the applied bearing pressure is held to at most **0.78 of the FS = 2.5 allowable** (the maximum reported ratio is 5.586/7.200 = 0.776), which is an effective factor of safety of **3.22**. This covers the stricter reading of the footnote while keeping the FS basis stated by the table transparent. The BOD's instruction to specify the lowest listed strength satisfying durability and structural demand is applied separately (see §7).

### 4.3 Groundwater correction

UFC 3-220-20 states: *"Groundwater correction is required when the groundwater table is higher than one footing width below the bearing elevation. Groundwater correction is only required for drained (effective stress) analysis."* Where applicable, the average effective unit weight in the failure zone was computed by EM 1110-1-1905 Eq. 1-6:

> *γ′_H = γ_sub + [(D_GWT − D)/H] γ_w*, with *H = B tan(45° + φ′/2)* and *γ_sub = γ_total − 62.4 pcf*.

The Data Report §2 requires the submerged unit weight to be taken as total less 62.4 pcf. The stabilised groundwater depths are 8.0 ft (P1), 9.0 ft (P2), 19.0 ft (P3), 8.0 ft (P4), 21.0 ft (P5), and 8.5 ft (P6) below finished grade (Civil grading and groundwater record §2). The correction is therefore active at P1, P2, P4 and P6, where the water table lies within one footing width of the base, and it is also active at the larger P3 and P5 footings, whose computed failure depth H = B tan(45° + φ′/2) reaches below the 19.0-ft and 21.0-ft water tables. Where the water table lies below H, total unit weights are used. The correction reduces, never increases, the computed capacity; the reported allowable values already include it.

### 4.4 Bearing stratum

The Data Report §4 requires the base of Stratum I to be interpolated **linearly between the two borings of the pad using the foundation station**, rounded to 0.1 ft, with no extrapolation outside the boring interval. The two borings of every pad are at the first and last foundation stations (0.0 and 77.0 ft), so every Phase 1 foundation lies between them and interpolation governs. The resulting Stratum I bases (ft) are:

| Pad | F1 | F2 | F3 | F4 | F5 | W1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | 6.0 | 8.0 | 9.7 | 11.1 | 12.1 | 12.5 |
| CR-P2 | 13.5 | 12.1 | 10.9 | 10.0 | 9.3 | 9.0 |
| CR-P3 | 5.5 | 6.0 | 6.4 | 6.7 | 6.9 | 7.0 |
| CR-P4 | 6.0 | 7.1 | 8.0 | 8.7 | 9.3 | 9.5 |
| CR-P5 | 4.5 | 4.8 | 5.1 | 5.3 | 5.4 | 5.5 |
| CR-P6 | 14.0 | 11.7 | 9.7 | 8.2 | 7.0 | 6.5 |

The adopted bearing depths put **all six pads in Stratum I** (the residual silt/lean clay). The declared `bearing_stratum` in the parameter file is therefore "I" for every foundation at every pad. This is consistent with the shared bearing elevation and the interpolated contacts: the deepest adopted bearing depth is 48 in (4.0 ft), and the shallowest Stratum I base is 4.5 ft (CR-P5 F1), so no foundation penetrates the Stratum I contact.

A deep Stratum II alternative was designed and priced for CR-P3 and CR-P5. It removes the compressible residual clay from the influence zone and reduces settlement, but it requires excavation of 7.0–7.5 ft at P3 and 6.0 ft at P5. When the neat excavation prism is measured correctly — vertical sides to 4 ft depth, then the civil 1.5H:1V slope below 4 ft, with 1 ft working room each side — the deep scheme costs more than the shallow spread scheme at both pads. At P3 the deep spread alternative was priced at $72,337 against $49,660 for the adopted shallow spread; at P5 the deep alternative was $38,451 against $29,922. The shallow-plus-piers alternatives are $57,275 at P3 and $34,069 at P5, also more than the adopted shallow spread. The adopted designs therefore remain in Stratum I, and the Stratum II properties (c′ = 0, φ′ = 33°, γ = 126 pcf, Es = 1700/1800 ksf) are used only for the alternative pricing, not for the selected bearing check.

## 5. Settlement method and tolerable-movement criteria

### 5.1 Method applied

RFI-019 is the governing instruction on settlement. It states, in full:

> *"Apply LAYERED ELASTIC COMPRESSION: divide the soil below the bearing surface into layers, compute the net stress increment in each layer with the 2 vertical to 1 horizontal approximate stress distribution for a rectangular loaded area, and sum the layer compressions s = (delta sigma)(H)/Es using the pad-specific elastic moduli of the geotechnical data report. This is the method the governing FHWA ground-modification reference states as Equation 5-14, and using it for the unimproved case keeps the improved and unimproved cases consistent, because the lower-zone term of the two-layer aggregate-pier method is the same equation. Carry the compression integral to a depth of four times the footing width below the bearing surface, and in no case less than 40 ft. Subdivide that depth into UNIFORM LAYERS 0.25 ft THICK and take the stress increment at the mid-height of each layer; that discretisation is fine enough that the computed compression is stable to better than one per cent. The subgrade-reaction estimator of the combined-footing and mat chapter of the foundations manual is not the settlement method for isolated spread footings on this project."*

The calculation applied is therefore:

* net applied pressure q = P_service/(B L), with P_service the D + L base reaction;
* 2V:1H stress increment Δσ(z) = q B L / [(B+z)(L+z)] for a rectangular loaded area;
* layers 0.25 ft thick from the bearing surface to max(4B, 40 ft);
* Es taken at the mid-height of each layer from the pad-specific Data Report values (Stratum I 85–250 ksf; Stratum II 1400–1800 ksf; Stratum III 1700–3800 ksf);
* s = Σ Δσ H / Es, with H = 0.25 ft.

For improved footings the FHWA GEC 13 two-layer method is used (Eqs. 5-11 to 5-14): total settlement s_tot = s_uz + s_lz; upper-zone settlement s_uz = q_g/k_g (Eq. 5-13); lower-zone settlement from the bottom of the treated zone to the same max(4B, 40 ft) depth by the same 2V:1H layered compression (Eq. 5-14). The top-of-pier stress is q_g = q n_s/(n_s − 1 + 1/R_a) (Eq. 5-12) with n_s = 10 and the actual footing area replacement ratio. The pad-specific stiffness moduli k_g are the Kettleridge §3 design values (P1 165, P2 140, P4 195, P6 155 pci). The upper-zone settlement is independent of the treatment depth; the treatment depth controls where the lower-zone integral starts, and depths of 8–12 ft were selected to reach or pass the Stratum I base so the lower zone is the stiff sand, not the residual clay.

### 5.2 Tolerable movement adopted

UFC 3-220-01 paragraph 2-4.7.1 states:

> *"Unless approved by the building official, total post construction settlement may not exceed tolerable limits based on building type and dimension, or 25.4 mm (1 in.), whichever is less. Differential settlements shall not result in an angular distortion in excess of 1/500. The angular distortion is defined as the difference in settlement between two points divided by the distance between the points."*

The adopted criteria are therefore **total settlement ≤ 1.0 in** and **angular distortion between adjacent foundation units ≤ 1/500 = 0.002**, using the station distances along the instrumented column line (24, 20, 16, 12 and 5 ft). The predicted maximum total settlement is **0.777 in** (CR-P2 F2), and the predicted maximum angular distortion is **0.00149** (CR-P1, F3–F4),

UFC 3-220-20

to the footing.  Considerations of settlement will control when punching shear is the 
dominant bearing capacity failure mode.  The term punching shear is also used by 
some to refer to the case of a footing punching through a thin layer of stiff consistency 
or dense soil into a soft consistency or loose soil below.  This mechanism is discussed 
in Section 5-3.6.  
As indicated by Figure 5-3(d), the general shear mechanism applies mostly to dense 
soils at relatively shallow depths.  At lower relative densities and greater footing depths, 
the failure mode transitions through local failure to punching shear.  The bearing 
capacity theories discussed in Section 5-3.1.2 assume a general shear failure 
mechanism.  Methods to account for local shear are discussed in Section 5-3.1.3.  
5-3.1.1 
Shear Strength for Bearing Capacity Analysis. 
Bearing capacity is controlled by the shear strength of the soil.  The type of shear 
strength parameters used in bearing capacity analyses depends on the field loading 
condition, soil type, and groundwater level.  Loads are typically applied to foundations 
over a period of time, such as when a building or a bridge is under construction.  This 
loading condition may represent drained or undrained loading depending on the type of 
soil being loaded and the length of time required to apply the load.   
In clean sands and gravels, drainage is almost instantaneous and does not practically 
depend on how long it takes to build the structure.  These soils only require effective 
stress analysis unless dynamic loading is anticipated.  If substantial fines are present, 
the possibility of developing an undrained condition should be considered. 
In contrast, substantial time is required for excess pore pressures to dissipate in fine-
grained soils after loading.  These soils usually require undrained analysis for conditions 
at the end of loading as well as for any rapid or dynamic loading.  In some cases, long-
term effective stress conditions should also be checked.  For example, the drained 
bearing capacity of heavily overconsolidated clays often controls the design. 
Laboratory and field testing methods to determine shear strength parameters for most 
soil types are summarized in the Prologue.  For bearing capacity analysis, effective 
strength parameters (φ ʹ, cʹ) should be used for long-term conditions in all soil types.  For 
saturated fine-grained soils, the use of undrained shear strength (su) with φ = 0 is 
appropriate.  Undrained shear strength parameters (φ, c) should be used for unsaturated 
soils with low permeability, including coarse-grained soils with substantial fines. 
5-3.1.2 
Calculation of Ultimate Bearing Capacity. 
Bearing capacity is a complex phenomenon that cannot be modeled exactly.  Multiple 
equations have been developed to estimate the ultimate bearing capacity of soil.  These 
equations are based on the upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity and include 


--- page 324 ---
UFC 3-220-20 
16 January 2025 
 
 
286 
the work of Prandtl (1920), Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1951), Brinch Hansen (1970), 
and Vesic (1973, 1975).  In their basic form, the equations apply to general shear failure 
below a continuous strip footing of width, B, with soil shear strength governed by the 
Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion.  The basic bearing capacity solutions also assume 
vertical loading, a horizontal bearing surface, foundation depth less than the width, and 
a horizontal ground surface.  Methods to address other variations of these factors are 
discussed in Section 5-3.3. 
In most methods, the bearing capacity problem is simplified by replacing the soil above 
the bearing elevation with an equivalent surcharge as shown in Figure 5-4(a).  This 
conservatively neglects the shear strength of the soil above the foundation depth.  
Alternatively, Meyerhof (1951) assumed that the failure surface continued to the ground 
surface and replaced the triangular wedge with equivalent stresses, p0 and s0.  
Meyerhof’s geometry is shown in Figure 5-4(b).  Basic formulations also assume that 
the groundwater table is deeper than the failure zone.

287

a) Terzaghi, Brinch Hansen, and Vesic Methods and b) Meyerhof Method 
With these assumptions, the bearing capacity problem can be separated into three 
distinct terms or superimposed sources of bearing resistance.  The first term is 
connected to the cohesion (or undrained shear strength) along the failure surface and 
has a bearing capacity factor, Nc.  The second term is related to the surcharge and has 
a bearing capacity factor, Nq.  The third term is related to the weight of the soil above 
the failure surface and has a bearing capacity factor, Nγ.

Groundwater Correction. 
Groundwater correction is required when the groundwater table is higher than one 
footing width below the bearing elevation.  Groundwater correction is only required for 
drained (effective stress) analysis.  Groundwater is considered by changing the unit 
weight used in the bearing capacity calculations.  The three possible cases are shown 
in Figure 5-6.  These cases assume hydrostatic conditions (i.e., no seepage forces 
exist).

Effects of Groundwater Table on Bearing Capacity Calculations 
For undrained analysis, total unit weights are used without regard to the position of the 
groundwater table. 
Uplift is present on the base of the foundation when the groundwater table is above the 
bearing elevation.  Its effect on the bearing pressure can be conservatively ignored 
unless sliding or uplift is a concern. 
 
Methods to Account for Complicating Effects. 
Multiple aspects of a foundation design can affect the bearing capacity that are not 
included in the basic solutions presented in Section 5-3.1.2.  These include foundation 
shape and depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination.  A shallow 
foundation with all three inclinations is illustrated in Figure 5-7. 
The correction methods in the following sections are based on both theoretical 
considerations and empirical evidence.  For this reason, the correction factors cannot 
usually be applied across methods, i.e., Meyerhof corrections should be used only with 
the Meyerhof bearing capacity factors.  In addition, care should be taken combining

For area wide ground improvement applications, the design method is identical to that 
previously detailed for stone columns. The stone within the rammed aggregate piers having 
been compacted by impact ramming typically exhibits a somewhat higher effective friction 
angle, in the range of 45 to 50 degrees, and potentially higher stiffness (modulus). 
Consequently, the ratio of the stiffness (modulus) of the rammed aggregate piers to the 
stiffness of the in situ soil should be somewhat higher than for stone columns, resulting in a 
higher design stress ratio than previously identified for stone columns. Although the Geopier 
design manual suggests stress ratios of 20 or higher, a stress ratio of 5 to 10 for area ground 
improvement applications under flexible embankment loading appears warranted until 
considerably more field data in support of a higher ratio is developed. 
For structure foundation support under rigid footings a somewhat higher stress ratio (10) may 
be considered, with anticipated settlements and pier capacity conventionally computed, based 
on the loads on each element. The load on the rammed aggregate pier and on the in situ soil 
is based on the chosen stress and replacement ratios. The design area replacement ratio is 
determined after evaluating settlement of the unimproved soil. A minimum replacement ratio 
of 0.33 is generally recommended, as noted in the HITEC Evaluation Report (Collin 2007). 
4.2.2 Design Procedures 
Rammed aggregate piers are typically selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce 
settlement, increase shear strength, or provide any combination of the above. 
Preliminary design methods and assumptions to achieve the desired end result are outlined in 
this section. 
The generalized design process for an embankment support is as follows: 
1. Perform embankment design without rammed aggregate piers to determine the overall 
settlement and global stability to determine if rammed aggregate piers or another 
form of ground improvement are required. If so proceed to step 2. 
2. Assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter. 
3. Determine the spacing based on the assumed area replacement ratio and column 
diameter.  
4. Check the load bearing resistance of the rammed aggregate pier to see if it meets the 
project requirements. If not revise the column diameter and re-check. 
5. Determine the total settlement of the embankment supported on rammed aggregate 
piers.

The design process for rammed aggregate piers is similar in many respects to stone columns. 
However, the major difference in design of the two systems is with respect to settlement 
analysis that is presented in the following sections.  
4.2.3 Settlement Analysis 
Rammed aggregate pier settlement control design methodology is based on a two-layer 
settlement approach as described by Lawton et al. (1994), Fox and Cowell (1998), and 
Wissmann et al. (2002). The installation of rammed aggregate piers within the aggregate 
column-reinforced zone, referred to as the upper zone, creates a stiffened, engineered zone 
with reduced compressibility that reduces settlement of embankments and transportation-
related structures. The settlement below the rammed aggregate pier-reinforced zone, referred 
to as the lower-zone, is evaluated using conventional geotechnical analysis approaches. The 
total settlement (stot) of the transportation structures is evaluated as the sum of the upper zone

import json
g=json.load(open('/tmp/review/x/foundation_geometry.json'))
fcmap={3000:182,4000:196,4500:211,5000:228}
tot_by_pad={}
tot=0
for pad,pd in g['pads'].items():
    s=0; nimp=0
    for tag,f in pd['foundations'].items():
        B=f['B_in']/12; L=f['L_in']/12; t=f['thickness_in']/12
        D=pd['bearing_depth_in']/12
        Vc=B*L*t
        conc=Vc*fcmap[pd['fc_psi']]
        rebar=2*f['reinforcement_ratio']*Vc*490*1.42
        exc=(B+2)*(L+2)*D
        back=max(exc-Vc,0)*46
        exc_cost=exc*38
        pier=f['pier_count']*f['pier_depth_ft']*28
        plat=(B*L)/9*2.4 if f['foundation_type']=='IMPROVED_SPREAD' else 0
        c=conc+rebar+exc_cost+back+pier+plat
        s+=c
        if f['foundation_type']=='IMPROVED_SPREAD': nimp+=1
    test=9500 if nimp>0 else 0
    tot_by_pad[pad]=(s,test,s+test)
    tot+=s+test
    print(f"{pad}: foundations ${s:,.2f} test ${test:,} pad ${s+test:,.2f}")
print(f"sum pads ${tot:,.2f}  + mobilisation ${40000*g['pads']['CR-P1'] and 2*40000:,} = ${tot+80000:,.2f}")
print('json campus', g['project']['campus_total_cost_usd'])
EOF

## 10. Campus programme and cost optimisation

### 10.1 Alternatives priced for each pad

For every pad, both alternatives were designed to the same criteria and priced at the project unit prices. The "spread-only" alternative is the least-cost all-spread scheme that satisfies bearing, minimum width, shear, frost and the movement limits; for P1, P2 and P6 a shallow spread-only scheme cannot satisfy settlement or angular distortion, so the least-cost compliant spread-only scheme is a deep, very-large-footing scheme that bears below the compressible Stratum I where needed, and its (higher) cost is reported. For P3 and P5 the spread-only alternative is the adopted shallow scheme at the frost minimum. The "improved" alternative is the least-cost scheme using rammed aggregate piers under the footings that need them, including the per-pad production test.

| Pad | Spread-only cost | Improved cost | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | $532,227 | **$94,325** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 6.0–12.5 ft thick and soft (Es 110 ksf); a compliant spread-only scheme requires deep founding and very large footings, far more expensive than piers. |
| CR-P2 | $410,781 | **$104,661** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 9.0–13.5 ft thick with Es 85 ksf; a compliant spread-only scheme is far more expensive than piers. |
| CR-P3 | **$49,660** | $57,275 | SPREAD | Stratum I is only 5.5–7.0 ft thick; the shallow spread scheme at the 42-in frost minimum satisfies settlement and angular distortion and is cheaper than both the shallow-plus-piers scheme and a deep Stratum II scheme (priced at $72,337). |
| CR-P4 | $62,507 | **$51,510** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Piers under the heavy interior footings are cheaper than the large spread footings needed to control settlement, and the pad uses spare rig capacity. |
| CR-P5 | **$29,922** | $34,069 | SPREAD | Stratum I is only 4.5–5.5 ft thick; the shallow spread scheme at the 42-in frost minimum is the least-cost compliant scheme. The deep Stratum II alternative is $38,451 and the shallow-plus-piers alternative is $34,069, both more expensive; FROST governs because nothing else is near binding. |
| CR-P6 | $194,054 | **$96,037** | IMPROVED_SPREAD | Stratum I is 6.5–14.0 ft thick with Es 95 ksf; piers are much cheaper than a deep spread-only scheme. |

The costs in this table are the **pad-level construction costs** (concrete, reinforcement, excavation, backfill, piers, working platform and the per-pad production test where improved). They exclude the campus rig mobilisation, which is added once in the campus total.

### 10.2 Rig programme

Kettleridge §4 states: *"Each mobilised rig can serve AT MOST 2 building pads within the Phase 1 milestone window. If more pads are to be improved than the mobilised rigs can serve in that window, an additional rig must be mobilised and paid for. Mobilisation is a lump sum per rig and is not prorated."*

Four pads are improved (P1, P2, P4 and P6). Two rigs are therefore mobilised: **RIG-1 serves CR-P1 and CR-P2; RIG-2 serves CR-P4 and CR-P6**. The mobilisation cost is 2 × $40,000 = **$80,000**. One production modulus test is required and priced for each improved pad; the plan reports one test per improved pad.

The campus programme was selected by comparing all subsets of the six pads at the priced alternatives and adding the correct number of rigs, `ceil(k/2)`, for k improved pads. The optimum is P1, P2, P4 and P6 improved, with P3 and P5 shallow spread at the 42-in frost minimum:

* P1, P2 and P6 must be improved because their spread-only alternatives are infeasible or far more expensive; three improved pads already require two rigs.
* P4 is improved because its improved cost ($51,510) is lower than its spread-only cost ($62,507) and it fits on the second rig with no additional mobilisation.
* P3 and P5 are not improved. Their improved alternatives ($57,275 and $34,069) are more expensive than their shallow spread alternatives ($49,660 and $29,922), and adding either would require a third rig ($40,000) because both rigs are already fully committed to P1, P2, P4 and P6. The $40,000 mobilisation is not justified by the direct saving.

### 10.3 Cost total

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| CR-P1 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $94,325 |
| CR-P2 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $104,661 |
| CR-P3 (shallow spread) | $49,660 |
| CR-P4 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $51,510 |
| CR-P5 (shallow spread) | $29,922 |
| CR-P6 (improved, incl. $9,500 test) | $96,037 |
| Rig mobilisation (2 × $40,000) | $80,000 |
| **Campus total** | **$506,116** |

The cost build-up uses the bid schedule Rev. 1 prices: concrete at $196/$211/$228 per CY for 4000/4500/5000 psi; reinforcement at $1.42/lb with the pay quantity = 2 × ratio × gross footing volume × 490 pcf; excavation at $38/CY to the neat prism (vertical sides for the selected D ≤ 4 ft, with the civil 1.5H:1V slope below 4 ft applied to the deeper alternatives) with 1 ft working room each side; backfill at $46/CY = excavation less concrete; dewatering at $4,200/day but zero days on every pad because all bearing surfaces are above the stabilised groundwater. The RAP prices are $28/LF, $2.40/SY of improved footing plan area, $9,500 per production test, and $40,000 per rig.

## 11. Pad-by-pad summary

| Pad | Bearing depth (in) | Bearing stratum | FS | Decision | Max settlement (in) | Max angular distortion | Max q_net/q_allow | Pad cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-P1 | 45 | I | 3.5 | IMPROVED_SPREAD | 0.637 | 0.00149 | 0.957 | $94,325 |
| CR-P2 | 45 | I | 3.5 | IMPROVED_SPREAD | 0.777 | 0.00144 | 0.951 | $104,661 |
| CR-P3 | 42 | I | 3.5 | SPREAD | 0.718 | 0.00137 | 0.918 | $49,660 |
| CR-P4 | 42 | I | 3.0 | IMPROVED_SPREAD | 0.562 | 0.00149 | 0.950 | $51,510 |
